materials.name: Lawn — tall fescue (sod)
materials.notes: Cool-season; the most drought- and shade-tolerant cool-season lawn. Northeast and the upper South. Seeding costs roughly a quarter of sod.

materials.name: Lawn — Kentucky bluegrass blend (sod)
materials.notes: Cool-season; spreads by rhizomes and self-repairs, but needs full sun and summer irrigation. Northeast.

materials.name: Lawn — bermudagrass (sod)
materials.notes: Warm-season; full sun only, very heat and wear tolerant, dormant tan in winter. Southeast and low desert.

materials.name: Lawn — zoysiagrass (sod)
materials.notes: Warm-season; dense and slow to establish, tolerates light shade better than bermudagrass. Southeast.

materials.name: Lawn — St. Augustinegrass (sod)
materials.notes: Warm-season, coarse-bladed; the usual shade-tolerant lawn in Florida and the Gulf Coast. Not cold hardy above zone 8.

materials.name: Lawn — buffalograss (plugs or sod)
materials.notes: Native warm-season prairie grass; needs a fraction of the water of other lawns, full sun, little traffic. High desert and plains.

materials.name: Shredded hardwood mulch (75 mm)
materials.notes: Knits together and stays on slopes. Top up 25 mm a year; keep 5–10 cm clear of trunks and stems.

materials.name: Pine straw (75 mm settled)
materials.notes: Southeastern standard. Light, stays put on slopes, breaks down in about a year.

materials.name: Pine bark nuggets (75 mm)
materials.notes: Long-lasting but floats and washes off slopes; use on level beds.

materials.name: Arborist wood chips (100 mm)
materials.notes: Coarse mixed chips; inexpensive or free locally. Good under trees and for informal paths.

materials.name: Pea gravel (75 mm)
materials.notes: Rounded and comfortable underfoot but migrates; needs edging and a compacted base for paths.

materials.name: Crushed stone, 19 mm (100 mm over base)
materials.notes: Angular stone locks together; the usual gravel driveway and path surface over geotextile and a compacted base.

materials.name: River rock, 25–75 mm
materials.notes: Dry creek beds and drainage swales; heat-retentive in sun, so avoid around tender plants in the low desert.

materials.name: Decomposed granite (stabilized, 75 mm)
materials.notes: Southwestern standard for paths and xeric beds. Stabilized DG resists erosion; plain DG is cheaper and better as mulch around cacti.

materials.name: Flagstone, dry-laid on sand and gravel
materials.notes: Bluestone in the Northeast, sandstone and limestone elsewhere. Mortared on a slab costs roughly 30–50 % more.

materials.name: Concrete pavers
materials.notes: Interlocking units on a compacted aggregate base; individual units can be lifted for repairs. Driveways need a thicker base.

materials.name: Permeable interlocking pavers
materials.notes: Open joints over an open-graded stone reservoir infiltrate rainwater; may count toward stormwater credits.

materials.name: Clay brick pavers
materials.notes: Use paving-grade brick, not wall brick, where freeze–thaw occurs.

materials.name: Poured concrete, broom finish
materials.notes: Lowest-cost permanent paving; plan control joints and slope 1–2 % away from buildings.

materials.name: Stamped or colored concrete
materials.notes: Patterned slab; needs periodic resealing and is slippery when wet if sealed glossy.

materials.name: Asphalt paving
materials.notes: Common residential driveway surface; sealcoat every few years. Hot underfoot and adds runoff.

materials.name: In-ground pool (plaster finish)
materials.notes: Planning figure per m² of water surface for a basic gunite or shotcrete pool; decking, fencing and equipment extra. Pool barriers are code-required.

materials.name: Lined garden pond
materials.notes: EPDM-lined pond with gravel edge; pump and filtration extra.

materials.name: Composite decking (with framing)
materials.notes: Capped composite boards on pressure-treated framing; low maintenance. Dark colours get very hot in full sun.

materials.name: Pressure-treated wood deck
materials.notes: Lowest-cost deck; needs sealing or stain every 2–3 years.

materials.name: Wood board privacy fence (1.8 m)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "board". Cedar or pressure-treated pine; check local height limits and pool-barrier rules.

materials.name: Vinyl privacy fence (1.8 m)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "board". No painting; can become brittle in extreme cold or UV.

materials.name: Wood picket fence (1.1 m)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "picket". Front-yard boundary; typically 0.9–1.2 m.

materials.name: Aluminum ornamental fence (1.5 m)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "metal". Common pool-code barrier; no rust.

materials.name: Chain-link fence (1.2 m, galvanized)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "metal". Vinyl-coated black or green reads less industrial.

materials.name: Split-rail fence (2–3 rail)
materials.notes: OpenPlan3D style "rail". Marks a boundary without screening; add welded wire to contain pets.

materials.name: Steel landscape edging
materials.notes: Style "steel". Thin, crisp line between lawn and bed; weathering steel rusts to a stable brown.

materials.name: Stone or cobble edging
materials.notes: Style "stone". Granite cobbles or cut stone set in concrete or compacted base.

materials.name: Plastic coil edging
materials.notes: Style "steel" equivalent at low cost; heaves in freeze–thaw unless staked every 1 m.

materials.name: Segmental concrete block retaining wall
materials.notes: Style "block". Walls over about 1.2 m, or carrying a driveway or slope above, need engineered geogrid and often a permit.

materials.name: Dry-laid natural stone retaining wall
materials.notes: Style "stone". Batter the face back and keep under about 1 m without engineering.
